source_document.body:
For many owner-operators, the hardest part of running a truck isn’t driving. It’s everything else: finding steady freight, managing costs, and carving out time for family. Richard Loya Jr., owner of Classic Trucking LLC, has spent the past six years learning all three, and he says the lesson that mattered most was realizing he had stopped being a driver and become a business owner.
Loya recently sat down for a special interview presented by Amazon Relay to talk about what the work looks like from the driver’s seat. He covered his path from warehouse floor to his own authority, how contract freight changed his business, and how he approaches the numbers that decide whether an owner-operator survives.
From the warehouse to the cab
Loya has held his CDL for eight years. Before that, he worked a string of jobs, mostly in warehousing and logistics in Southern California, where he said that kind of work is “what you got to go with.” He spent most of his warehouse career selecting orders, including a stint in the freezer that he admits didn’t suit him. “I’m a tropical person,” he said. “I like the heat.”
He eventually moved into driving for the same company, running deliveries to fast-food restaurants and offloading 48-foot trailers himself. The job also meant key drops, opening stores and shutting off alarms in the early hours. He recalled one 4 a.m. stop in East Los Angeles when the alarm wouldn’t quit and cars began pulling up to watch. It was grueling work, and it came with a schedule that kept him from ordinary life. Working nights and weekends meant he rarely saw daylight and was too tired on Sundays to enjoy his one day off.
Friends who had already made the jump into trucking kept telling him the same thing: if he was going to work that hard, he should do it for himself. When COVID hit in 2020, he was running routes and staying overnight up north, and the logic finally clicked. “If I’m going to be doing all this work, I might as well do it myself,” he said. He saved up, bought a truck, and started his own authority.
Trading brokers for stability
For his first couple of years, Loya hauled through a broker, and he found the arrangement unpredictable. Some weeks there was freight, and some weeks there wasn’t. “You’re doing the hard work, being on time, being safe, doing everything you need to do, and then for them to not at least give you the opportunity to work,” he said. The inconsistency, he added, was “messing up the flow.”
A friend suggested he try Amazon Relay. Once he learned how the platform worked, he said, things improved quickly. The biggest change was a sense of control. “It puts it in my hands,” Loya said. “I’m not relying on a broker to find work. Now it’s all on me. I’m going to rise or fall. It’s my choice, and that’s kind of what I wanted when I bought my own truck.”
His days now are simpler. Much of the work is dropping and hooking trailers, and he can concentrate on being on time and safe. For Loya, that consistency mattered during the freight recession, when many carriers left the industry. “I have always been able to find work with Relay” he said. “There are a lot of people who are just looking for the opportunity to work, and it’s there.”
It has also shaped how he balances work and home, particularly with a two-year-old and a 20-year-old daughter. Loya described two ways to work with Relay. For Loya, contracts offer predictable, recurring freight, while the load board offers flexibility when something comes up with family. “That day I’m not going to take a contract, I’m going to put something on the load board and build my week out however I can make it work,” he said. Some weeks he takes loads that keep him close to home, and others he goes out to earn more. “It’s about finding the balance.”
At Amazon’s RelayCon in Las Vegas, Loya said he took away a simple message about contract freight. “The contracts are really the stability part,” he said. “. If you want to have the consistency, for sure, contracts are right.”
Doing the math on every load
Having freight to haul doesn’t mean every load is a good one, and Loya is blunt about what it takes to stay profitable. He handles permits, insurance, and maintenance himself, and he runs the numbers before accepting a run. Fuel is the largest expense, and he knows California prices are among the highest in the country. To keep that cost down, he uses a fuel card at smaller, more local chains that offer discounts, rather than at the big national stops.
Deadhead miles come first when he evaluates a load. “It’s a big one,” he said. “I have everything pre-factored in my head. When I’m looking at something, I’ve got to know the cost per mile. I do a quick addition of how many miles, and see if it makes sense for me.” He knows his insurance costs, fuel costs, and maintenance costs, and he builds each load decision around them.
He also keeps several mechanics on call, since the best shop is often the busiest one when something breaks. “You gotta have two, three, maybe even four that you can go to if something happens,” he said. The host noted that this is easier to do in a large market like Los Angeles than in more rural parts of the country.
Learning the business side
Loya’s approach to growth is to keep learning from everyone he meets. He treats events like RelayCon as a chance to hear what other owner-operators are dealing with and to take something back to his own operation. “I try to learn a little bit from different people and kind of build my own,” he said.
He applies the same mindset to overhead. When his insurance renews, he calls around to five different providers and asks for a breakdown of the rate. “Sometimes they’ll even go a lot lower, and you don’t even realize it,” he said. “You’re kind of negotiating in a way. They want your business.”
That discipline reflects a distinction, being a good driver and being a good business owner are different skills, and the second doesn’t develop automatically. FreightWaves Editorial Director and former driver, Adam Wingfield said, “You have to be intentional about getting better at business,” noting that an operation that only moves when its owner is behind the wheel is difficult to build on, or to leave to anyone else.
Loya said he feels that gap. “Don’t be so focused on just driving as a job. You’re running the whole business, even if it’s one truck,” he said. “I’ve got to gain the knowledge first.”
Something to leave behind
The knowledge matters because of what Loya wants Classic Trucking to become. He wants to leave the company to both of his daughters. “I wanted it to be something I could leave to both of them and have it established, and they just take over,” he said. “I think they have a leg up on things. I started from scratch.”
He acknowledges he is still working out how to get there, and he doesn’t pretend to have it figured out. But his plan is to keep experimenting, including with other opportunities within Amazon Relay that he hasn’t tried yet. “Don’t be scared to try it out,” he said. “If it doesn’t work, go back to what you know. Sometimes those new opportunities will show you something that works out pretty good.”
His advice for other operators was brief. “Anything worth doing takes time,” Loya said. “It’s not easy all the time, but you’ve got to stick with it.”
Individual carrier experiences vary. Amazon Relay does not guarantee load volume or availability.
